slides.title: A valid address is not a valid object access
keyPoints: Capacity, received extent, and lifetime are separate limits
The OS protects pages, not every C++ object boundary
Repair the first invalid operation
slides.narration: A pointer can designate a mapped writable page and still be invalid for the object or range a program intends to use. A large buffer may have capacity for one thousand bytes while only seven bytes were received. A freed object may leave plausible-looking bits at its former address. Neither situation authorizes reading or writing those bytes as live input. Memory safety requires the correct extent and lifetime at each access. This chapter studies those boundaries with safe demonstrations and checked arithmetic. We will not deliberately execute an overflow or use-after-free and then treat one observed outcome as a guarantee.

question.prompt: Why does a writable page not prove that a copy stays within its destination object?
question.answer: Several objects can share a page. Page permissions do not enforce the allocation or array boundary of each C++ object.

slides.title: A narrowing conversion can hide an oversized request
keyPoints: 250 payload units plus 10 header units need 260
An explicit 8-bit conversion produces 4
Validate before narrowing or allocating
slides.narration: This demonstration legally converts the number two hundred sixty to an eight-bit unsigned type, producing four modulo two hundred fifty-six. It does not allocate four bytes and copy two hundred fifty into them; that unsafe operation is deliberately absent. The printed wrapped total shows how a bad size pipeline could under-allocate. The checked decision compares the payload against maximum minus header before addition and rejects the request. Use one validated representation for both allocation and the later copy. Checking a narrowed size while retaining the original large copy length creates two conflicting meanings for the same request.

question.answer: No. It demonstrates legal unsigned narrowing losing the required size. The later unsafe copy is not performed; validation rejects the request.

slides.title: A safe observer asks whether ownership still exists
keyPoints: weak_ptr does not keep the target alive
lock obtains an owner only while the object exists
After the owner ends, reject access instead of dereferencing stale memory
slides.narration: The observer refers weakly to a string created inside a scope. While the strong owner exists, expired is false and the program prints alive equals one. When the scope ends, the only strong owner is destroyed and the object dies. The later lock cannot obtain an owner, so the program prints expired equals one and unavailable. No freed string is accessed. This is one possible lifetime design, not a command to use shared ownership everywhere. A shorter borrowed reference with a guaranteed enclosing owner can be simpler. Shared ownership also does not synchronize concurrent changes to the string itself.

question.prompt: What lifetime guarantee does a successful weak_ptr::lock provide?
question.answer: It returns a shared owner that keeps the target alive while that owner is retained. It does not automatically protect mutable contents from races.

slides.title: Validate received bytes rather than allocated capacity
keyPoints: The header must already exist before decoding
The payload must fit the received remainder
The application maximum is an additional check
slides.narration: Suppose a receive buffer has capacity sixty-four bytes but the latest valid input extent is only five. A two-byte header claiming four payload bytes does not fit: only three payload bytes have arrived. Capacity cannot supply the missing fourth byte. The parser first proves the header exists, then enforces the application maximum, then compares the payload length with received minus header. Short-circuit evaluation makes that subtraction safe only after the header bound holds. This order also avoids an overflowing header-plus-payload expression. Once validation succeeds, use that same checked extent when constructing a view or copying data.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
keyPoints: Checking header_size + claimed_payload <= buffer_size can wrap if unchecked size_t inputs are large. Passing a wrapped check can lead to an undersized buffer.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Compare against buffer capacity rather than the number of bytes actually received. Uninitialized or stale bytes can be mistaken for input.
The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Carry valid extent with the data and validate against it. Keep allocation capacity as a separate property.

slides.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
keyPoints: A parser needs both a received-extent check and an application resource limit. A large backing allocation does not imply that unread bytes are valid input, and a valid extent does not authorize an arbitrarily large message. Short-circuit evaluation ensures subtraction occurs only after the header is known to fit.
A plausible alternative: A bounded view carrying pointer and length reduces mismatched arguments; it does not remove the need for correct validation.

The defensive objective is to prevent invalid operations before they occur.
Page permissions and hardening features are valuable secondary barriers, but they do not replace length validation, checked arithmetic, lifetime management, and synchronization.

slides.title: Buffer overflows
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A buffer overflow writes beyond a buffer’s valid extent.
The immediate cause can be an unchecked length, a missing terminator allowance, a wrong element-size calculation, or a parser that trusts a field before validating it.
Tie every byte operation to an explicit extent.
For a destination of capacity c and requested copy length n , prove n <= c before copying.
slides.narration: A buffer overflow writes beyond a buffer’s valid extent. Tie every byte operation to an explicit extent. For a destination of capacity c and requested copy length n , prove n <= c before copying. For a string requiring a terminator, include that byte in the contract without computing an overflowing n + 1 . A length-aware interface helps, but its supplied lengths must still be correct.

keyPoints: This parser accepts a two-byte big-endian length followed by exactly that many payload bytes, with a maximum payload of 16 bytes.

slides.narration: This parser accepts a two-byte big-endian length followed by exactly that many payload bytes, with a maximum payload of 16 bytes. It returns a borrowed view, so the input owner must remain alive while the result is used. No allocation depends on the untrusted length. Companion listing: ch57/parse_frame.cpp The validation order is deliberate. First prove that the prefix bytes exist. Then decode into a type wide enough for the field. Next enforce the application maximum. Finally compare the remaining input length without an unchecked addition. Only after all checks does the parser create the payload view. The strict equality rejects trailing bytes because this function parses exactly one complete frame. A streaming parser would instead retain unconsumed bytes and return a consumed-length result. Changing that contract requires a deliberate interface change, not silently ignoring extra data.

slides.title: Exactly one frame and one frame from a stream are different APIs
keyPoints: A complete-frame parser can reject trailing bytes
A streaming parser returns a consumed count
Do not silently switch the contract
slides.narration: The source complete-frame parser requires the two-byte length to match exactly the remaining input, so trailing bytes are rejected. keyPoints: Local arrays have exact valid bounds
Neighbor order can change with compilation
An apparent padding overwrite is still invalid
slides.narration: A local array of thirty-two bytes cannot safely receive forty unchecked bytes. On one build the extra writes might appear to touch unused padding; on another they may affect another variable or implementation-managed state. C++ does not make out-of-bounds access valid because an experiment seems harmless. Optimizations and stack layout can change what symptoms appear, and undefined behavior removes the reliable source-level reasoning we need. The repair is to prove the destination extent before writing, including terminator requirements where relevant. A canary or sanitizer can detect some failures, but neither changes the original bound.

slides.title: A heap failure may be a delayed symptom
keyPoints: An earlier write can damage another allocation
A later allocation or free may expose the damage
Trace the first invalid access, not just the final crash
slides.narration: Heap corruption can surface far from its origin. One request writes past its buffer, damaging an adjacent object or allocator bookkeeping. A later unrelated allocation then fails or crashes. Patching the allocator call that finally reports trouble may leave the original write untouched. Reduce the failing case, enable suitable instrumentation, and trace the earliest invalid operation. Keep ownership and extents visible at interfaces so the defect can be narrowed to a specific promise. The operating system may permit the machine write because the surrounding page is writable, even while the language-level object access is already invalid.

question.prompt: Why is a crash during free not proof that free caused the original defect?

slides.title: Validate sign and multiplication before converting a size
keyPoints: A negative signed value can become a huge unsigned size
count × element size can overflow

slides.narration: An external count should be validated before converting it to an allocation size. If a signed negative count becomes size_t first, it may turn into a very large positive value. For multiplication, a nonzero element size lets us check count against maximum divided by element size before forming the product. The same validated count should then control construction and copying. Re-parsing the field or recomputing it in a narrower type can reintroduce disagreement. slides.title: An owner cannot protect every observer automatically
keyPoints: unique_ptr prevents duplicate exclusive ownership
Raw pointers derived from it can still dangle after reset
A borrowed view needs an explicit enclosing lifetime
slides.narration: Owning abstractions make release responsibility clearer, but they do not repair every borrowed pointer. A raw pointer obtained from unique_ptr becomes invalid when its object is reset or destroyed. A string_view returned by a parser similarly depends on its input owner's lifetime and on changes that may invalidate storage. The complete-frame source deliberately returns a borrowed view, so its caller must keep the input alive while using it. If the result must outlive the input, return owned data or transfer an owner. Choose the least complicated lifetime model that actually supports the caller's use.

keyPoints: Test missing header, short body, and maximum allowed length

slides.narration: A useful parser test matrix follows the validation order. Supply fewer bytes than the header requires, a complete header with a short body, an exact maximum-size message, an oversized length, and trailing bytes when the API forbids them. Lifetime tests should observe release or failed ownership acquisition safely, as the weak observer demonstration does, rather than run a freed-pointer access and expect one fixed symptom. Instrumented runs add evidence, but a clean run covers only executed paths. Preserve the explicit checks in ordinary release builds where untrusted input still reaches the program.
